name: Tech Troubleshooter Framework
description: An interactive reference for diagnosing and repairing Windows and Mac computers. Built for technicians, power users, and anyone who wants to troubleshoot their own machine. Click any branch to expand it. Click any leaf node (○) to see full details, commands, and step-by-step instructions.

children.name: Windows
children.description: Troubleshooting tools, commands, and step-by-step solutions for Windows 10 and Windows 11. Covers system repair, networking, hardware, performance, security, and more.

children.name: System Repair
children.description: Core utilities for scanning and repairing corrupted Windows system files and images. The golden rule: always run DISM before SFC.

children.name: SFC (System File Checker)
children.description: Scans and repairs protected Windows system files using the Component Store as its source. Run AFTER DISM has completed successfully.

children.name: sfc /scannow
children.description: Scans ALL protected system files for corruption and replaces any corrupted or missing files with a cached copy from the Component Store. This is the most commonly used SFC command. Must be run as Administrator.

children.name: sfc /verifyonly
children.description: Scans system files but does NOT repair them. Use this when you want to detect problems without making any changes — safe to run on systems with custom configurations.

children.name: SFC in Safe Mode
children.description: If sfc /scannow fails to fix corruption in normal mode, boot into Safe Mode and run it again. Safe Mode prevents other programs from locking files that SFC needs to replace.
children.warning: Boot into Safe Mode first: Hold Shift + Restart → Troubleshoot → Advanced Options → Startup Settings → Restart → F4

children.name: DISM
children.description: Deployment Image Servicing and Management. Repairs the Windows Component Store (WinSxS) — the master blueprint SFC uses to repair files. Always run DISM before SFC. Requires internet or an ISO as source.

children.name: CheckHealth
children.description: Instantly checks if the system has already flagged itself as corrupted. Does NOT run a scan — reads an existing log. Takes under 1 second. Reports: Healthy, Repairable, or Non-Repairable.

children.name: ScanHealth
children.description: Thorough scan of the Component Store for corruption not yet flagged. Does NOT fix anything — only detects. Takes 5–10 minutes. Look for the message: 'The component store is repairable.'

children.name: RestoreHealth
children.description: The main repair command. Downloads healthy replacement files from Windows Update and repairs the Component Store. The progress bar may appear stuck at 20% or 40% for a long time — this is normal. Do not cancel.
children.warning: If this fails with Error 0x800f081f — use 'RestoreHealth with ISO'

children.name: RestoreHealth with ISO
children.description: Use when RestoreHealth fails because Windows Update is unavailable or corrupted. Provide a local Windows ISO as source. Steps: 1) Download ISO via Media Creation Tool. 2) Double-click ISO to mount it (note drive letter e.g. E:). 3) Find index number with Get-WimInfo. 4) Run command below. /LimitAccess forces DISM to use only the ISO.

children.name: AnalyzeComponentStore
children.description: Checks the size of the WinSxS folder and reports whether component cleanup is recommended. Use when low on disk space. Look for: 'Component Store Cleanup Recommended: Yes'

children.name: StartComponentCleanup
children.description: Deletes obsolete and superseded Windows update files to reclaim disk space and reduce corruption risk. Only run if AnalyzeComponentStore recommended cleanup.

children.name: ResetBase
children.description: Extreme cleanup — permanently makes all currently installed updates the new baseline. Saves the most disk space but you CANNOT uninstall existing updates afterward. Use only when necessary.
children.warning: IRREVERSIBLE: Existing updates cannot be uninstalled after this.

children.name: RevertPendingActions
children.description: Clears the 'pending.xml' file that queues update actions. Use when Windows is stuck in a boot loop saying 'Getting Windows Ready' or endlessly rebooting after an update.
children.warning: If Windows won't boot, run this from the Recovery Environment.

children.name: Remove Stuck Update
children.description: Removes a specific Windows update package by name when it can't be uninstalled via Settings. Step 1: List all packages to find the name. Step 2: Copy the exact package name. Step 3: Remove it.

children.name: Get-WimInfo
children.description: Lists all Windows editions inside a WIM or ESD file with their index numbers. Use to find the correct index (e.g. Index 6 = Windows 11 Pro) before running RestoreHealth with a local ISO source.

children.name: Convert ESD to WIM
children.description: Some Windows installation media uses install.esd instead of install.wim. DISM works better with WIM format. Convert using export-image. Prerequisites: Copy install.esd to C:\ESD first, open Admin CMD, cd C:\ESD
children.warning: Replace SourceIndex:1 with your edition's actual index from Get-WimInfo.

children.name: DISM Error Codes
children.description: Common DISM failure codes — all mean DISM cannot find or download source files.

children.name: Error 0x800f081f
children.description: Source files could not be found. DISM cannot locate repair files on Windows Update. Fix: Use RestoreHealth with a local ISO, or apply the Group Policy fix (gpedit.msc → Computer Configuration → Administrative Templates → System → 'Specify settings for optional component installation' → Enable → check 'Download repair content directly from Windows Update').

children.name: Error 0x800f0906
children.description: Source files could not be downloaded. Usually caused by a network block, firewall, or WSUS (corporate update server) interference. Fix: Apply the Group Policy fix or use ISO as source.

children.name: Error 0x800f0907
children.description: DISM is blocked by Group Policy. A policy prevents DISM from downloading repair content. Open gpedit.msc → Computer Configuration → Administrative Templates → System → 'Specify settings for optional component installation and component repair' → Set to Enabled → Check 'Download repair content directly from Windows Update instead of WSUS'.

children.name: PowerShell Method
children.description: Modern PowerShell alternative to CMD-based DISM. Repair-WindowsImage returns structured objects enabling scripted automation. Open PowerShell as Administrator before running any of these.

children.name: Check Health (PS)
children.description: PowerShell equivalent of DISM /CheckHealth. Returns ImageHealthState: Healthy or Repairable.

children.name: Scan Health (PS)
children.description: PowerShell equivalent of DISM /ScanHealth. Shows a cyan progress bar which is often more accurate than the CMD blinking cursor.

children.name: Restore Health (PS)
children.description: PowerShell equivalent of DISM /RestoreHealth.

children.name: Mount ISO (PS)
children.description: Mounts a Windows ISO automatically and stores the drive letter in a variable — no manual browsing needed.

children.name: Restore with ISO (PS)
children.description: Runs RestoreHealth using the mounted ISO. -LimitAccess prevents Windows Update use. Replace 6 with your index number.
children.warning: Do NOT put a space after WIM: — 'WIM: E:\...' will fail.

children.name: All-In-One Repair Script
children.description: Save as Repair-PC.ps1, run as Admin. Auto-detects corruption, restores if needed, then always runs SFC at the end.

children.name: Blue Screen (BSOD)
children.description: The Blue Screen of Death indicates a critical system error that forces Windows to stop. Always record the STOP code and the file name shown on the blue screen before troubleshooting.

children.name: Read the BSOD Code
children.description: When a BSOD occurs, Windows shows a STOP code (e.g. CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED) and sometimes a filename (e.g. ntfs.sys). Write both down. In Windows 11, the QR code on the BSOD links to Microsoft's support page for that exact error.
steps: Photograph or write down the STOP code and file name
Note what you were doing when it crashed
Check Event Viewer: eventvwr.msc → Windows Logs → System

children.name: Check Event Viewer
children.description: Event Viewer records detailed crash logs. Navigate to Windows Logs → System and look for Critical or Error level events around the time of the crash.
steps: Open eventvwr.msc as Admin
Navigate to Windows Logs → System
Click Filter Current Log → Level: Critical, Error
Find events at the time of the crash

children.name: Windows Memory Diagnostic
children.description: Faulty RAM is a very common cause of BSODs. Windows has a built-in memory test that runs on restart and checks for RAM errors.
steps: Run mdsched.exe as Admin
Choose 'Restart now and check for problems'
After restart: check results in Event Viewer → Windows Logs → System → search 'MemoryDiagnostics-Results'

children.name: Update or Roll Back Drivers
children.description: Driver conflicts are the #1 cause of BSODs. If the crash started after a driver update, roll it back. If drivers are old, update them.
steps: Open devmgmt.msc (Device Manager)
Look for any devices with a yellow ! warning icon
Right-click problematic device → Properties → Driver tab
Click 'Roll Back Driver' if available, otherwise 'Update Driver'
For graphics/GPU: download driver directly from NVIDIA/AMD/Intel website

children.name: Check for Overheating
children.description: Thermal throttling and overheating can cause random BSODs. Use HWMonitor or Core Temp to check CPU/GPU temperatures. CPU should be under 90°C under load; GPU under 85°C.
steps: Download HWMonitor or Core Temp (free tools)
Run a stress test (Prime95 for CPU) while monitoring temps
If temps exceed safe range: clean dust from vents/fans, replace thermal paste
Laptops: ensure vents are not blocked, use on hard surfaces

children.name: Run SFC and DISM
children.description: Corrupted system files are a common cause of BSODs. Run the standard system repair sequence.

children.name: Analyze Minidump Files
children.description: Windows saves small crash dump files (minidumps) when a BSOD occurs. Analyze them with WinDbg to find the exact driver or module that caused the crash.
steps: Open File Explorer → C:\Windows\Minidump
Download WinDbg from Microsoft Store
Open WinDbg → File → Open Crash Dump → select .dmp file
Type: !analyze -v in the command window
Look for the 'Probably caused by:' line

children.name: Common BSOD Codes
children.description: Reference for the most common BSOD stop codes and their meanings.

children.name: CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED
children.description: A critical Windows process (like winlogon.exe or csrss.exe) unexpectedly terminated. Causes: corrupted system files, faulty drivers, malware. Fix: Run SFC/DISM, scan for malware, check for driver updates.

children.name: SYSTEM_THREAD_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED
children.description: A kernel-mode driver or component threw an exception it couldn't handle. The filename shown on the BSOD identifies the driver. Fix: Update, roll back, or uninstall the driver shown.

children.name: MEMORY_MANAGEMENT
children.description: Serious error in Windows memory management. Often caused by faulty RAM, corrupted virtual memory settings, or corrupt system files. Fix: Run mdsched.exe (Memory Diagnostic), then SFC/DISM.

children.name: PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA
children.description: System tried to access memory that doesn't exist or was paged out. Causes: bad RAM, corrupted drivers, antivirus conflicts. Fix: Run Memory Diagnostic, update drivers, disable antivirus temporarily.

children.name: DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL
children.description: A driver accessed a memory address at an incorrect IRQL level. Almost always a driver issue. Note the driver filename shown on the BSOD and update or reinstall that specific driver.

children.name: IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL
children.description: Similar to DRIVER_IRQL — kernel-mode process tried to access a pageable memory address at too high an IRQL. Fix: Update all drivers, especially network and graphics drivers.

children.name: KERNEL_DATA_INPAGE_ERROR
children.description: Windows couldn't read data from virtual memory (page file). Indicates a bad hard drive, RAM, or corrupted page file. Fix: Run chkdsk C: /f /r, then Memory Diagnostic.

children.name: NTFS_FILE_SYSTEM
children.description: Error in the NTFS file system driver (ntfs.sys). Usually indicates a failing hard drive or corrupted file system. Fix: Run chkdsk C: /f /r from Recovery, then SFC/DISM.

children.name: WHEA_UNCORRECTABLE_ERROR
children.description: Hardware error detected by Windows Hardware Error Architecture. Causes: overclocking instability, failing CPU, bad RAM, overheating. Fix: Reset BIOS to default, reseat RAM, check CPU temps, run Memory Diagnostic.

children.name: DRIVER_POWER_STATE_FAILURE
children.description: A driver failed to respond properly to a power-state-change request (sleep, hibernate, or shutdown). Almost always a driver issue, often a graphics, network, or chipset driver. Disable Fast Startup as a first step.
steps: Disable Fast Startup: open Admin CMD → run: powercfg /h off
Update GPU and network drivers from the manufacturer's website
Update or roll back drivers shown in WhoCrashed or BlueScreenView pointing to a specific .sys file
Run Device Manager → look for any driver with a yellow warning icon and update it

children.name: BAD_POOL_HEADER
children.description: A pool header is corrupt — Windows detected memory corruption in the kernel pool. Almost always caused by faulty RAM, corrupted drivers, or sometimes a failing disk. Run Memory Diagnostic first.
steps: Run Windows Memory Diagnostic: Win+R → mdsched.exe → restart and test
Update or uninstall recently installed drivers
Boot into Safe Mode → if stable, a third-party driver is the cause
Run sfc /scannow then DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
Check disk: chkdsk C: /f /r

children.name: INACCESSIBLE_BOOT_DEVICE
children.description: Windows lost access to the system partition during startup. Common after BIOS changes, storage controller driver changes, cloned disks, or after major Windows updates. Boot to Recovery and run startup repair or rebuild BCD.
steps: Boot from Windows installation USB → Repair your computer → Troubleshoot → Advanced options → Startup Repair
If that fails: open Command Prompt from Recovery → run: chkdsk C: /f /r
Rebuild boot configuration: bootrec /fixmbr → bootrec /fixboot → bootrec /rebuildbcd
In BIOS/UEFI: verify SATA mode is correct (AHCI vs RAID) — changing modes mid-install causes this error
If after a Windows update: boot to Recovery → Uninstall Updates

children.name: UNEXPECTED_KERNEL_MODE_TRAP
children.description: The CPU generated an exception the kernel didn't catch — typically a double fault. Causes: faulty RAM, overclocking instability, or hardware-related driver bugs. Reset BIOS to defaults and run Memory Diagnostic first.
steps: Reset BIOS to factory defaults — disable any CPU/RAM overclocking
Run Windows Memory Diagnostic (mdsched.exe) — bad RAM is a top cause
Reseat RAM modules physically (Intel desktops with removable RAM)
Update chipset and BIOS firmware from the motherboard manufacturer
Check CPU temperatures under load — overheating triggers this on stressed systems

children.name: Safe Mode Troubleshooting
children.description: Boot into Safe Mode to diagnose BSODs. Safe Mode loads only essential drivers — if the BSOD stops in Safe Mode, a third-party driver or startup program is the cause.
steps: Hold Shift + click Restart in Start menu
Troubleshoot → Advanced Options → Startup Settings → Restart
Press F4 for Safe Mode or F5 for Safe Mode with Networking
In Safe Mode: uninstall recent drivers or software
If stable in Safe Mode: run msconfig → Selective Startup to isolate the cause

children.name: Network Troubleshooting
children.description: Step-by-step diagnosis and fixes for network connectivity issues — from basic no-internet errors to advanced DNS and TCP/IP problems.

children.name: No Internet Connection
children.description: Start here for any internet connectivity issue. Work through these steps in order before using advanced commands.
steps: Restart router and modem (unplug 30 seconds, plug back in)
Restart the computer
Try a different browser or device to isolate the issue
Check if other devices on the same network have internet
Right-click the network icon in taskbar → Troubleshoot Problems
Run: ipconfig /release then ipconfig /renew
Run: ipconfig /flushdns

children.name: Wi-Fi Keeps Disconnecting
children.description: Wi-Fi that drops intermittently is often caused by power management settings, outdated Wi-Fi drivers, or router channel congestion.
children.command:
netsh winsock reset
netsh int ip reset
ipconfig /flushdns
steps: Update Wi-Fi adapter driver via Device Manager
Disable Wi-Fi adapter power saving: Device Manager → Wi-Fi adapter → Properties → Power Management → uncheck 'Allow computer to turn off this device to save power'
Change router channel from 2.4GHz to 5GHz (or vice versa)
Forget and reconnect to the network
Reset network settings with netsh commands below
children.warning: Restart the computer after running netsh reset commands.

children.name: ipconfig Commands
children.description: IP Configuration commands — the foundation of network troubleshooting in Windows.

children.name: ipconfig /all
children.description: Shows detailed info for ALL network adapters: IP address, MAC address, DHCP server, DNS servers, gateway, lease times.

children.name: ipconfig /release + /renew
children.description: Releases the current DHCP IP address and requests a new one. The classic fix for 'can't get an IP address' problems.

children.name: ipconfig /flushdns
children.description: Clears the DNS resolver cache. Use when websites load with old/wrong content or when DNS changes aren't taking effect.

children.name: netsh Commands
children.description: Network Shell — powerful utility for resetting deep network stack components. Use when basic ipconfig fixes don't work.

children.name: Winsock Reset
children.description: Resets the Winsock Catalog — Windows's database of network settings used by all applications. Fixes a wide range of connectivity issues. Think of it as a factory reset for your network stack.
children.warning: Must restart the computer after this command.

children.name: TCP/IP Stack Reset
children.description: Resets the TCP/IP protocol stack to factory defaults. Fixes IP address conflicts and TCP/IP configuration corruption.
children.warning: Must restart the computer after this command.

children.name: Full Network Reset (All-in-One)
children.command:
netsh winsock reset
netsh int ip reset
ipconfig /release
ipconfig /renew
ipconfig /flushdns
children.description: Run all five commands in sequence for a complete network stack reset. This resolves the majority of software-based network issues.
children.warning: Restart the computer after running all five commands.

children.name: DNS Troubleshooting
children.description: DNS issues cause websites to fail to load even when the internet connection itself is working.

children.name: nslookup
children.description: Queries your DNS server to find the IP address for a domain. If this fails, DNS is broken. If it succeeds, the problem is elsewhere.

children.name: Change DNS to Google
children.command:
netsh interface ip set dns "Wi-Fi" static 8.8.8.8
netsh interface ip add dns "Wi-Fi" 8.8.4.4 index=2
children.description: Changes your DNS servers to Google's public DNS (8.8.8.8 and 8.8.4.4). Useful when your ISP's DNS is slow or broken. Replace 'Wi-Fi' with your actual adapter name from ipconfig /all.

children.name: Change DNS to Cloudflare
children.command:
netsh interface ip set dns "Wi-Fi" static 1.1.1.1
netsh interface ip add dns "Wi-Fi" 1.0.0.1 index=2
children.description: Changes DNS to Cloudflare (1.1.1.1) — the fastest public DNS resolver. Replace 'Wi-Fi' with your adapter name from ipconfig /all.

children.name: Ping & Tracert
children.description: Basic connectivity testing tools to determine where a network failure is occurring.

children.name: ping
children.description: Tests basic connectivity. If 'ping google.com' fails but 'ping 8.8.8.8' works, the problem is DNS. If both fail, the internet connection itself is broken.

children.name: tracert
children.description: Traces the path packets take to reach a destination, showing every router hop with response times. Identify WHERE on the path a connection is failing — timeout (*) at a specific hop indicates that router is the issue.

children.name: netstat
children.description: Displays all active TCP connections and listening ports in numerical format. Use to identify which programs are making connections and spot suspicious open ports.

children.name: Audio Issues
children.description: Troubleshooting no sound, distorted audio, microphone problems, and audio driver issues in Windows.

children.name: No Sound (Basic Checks)
children.description: Work through these basic checks before advanced troubleshooting.
steps: Check volume mixer: right-click speaker icon → Open Volume Mixer
Check that correct output device is selected: Settings → Sound → Output
Right-click speaker icon → Troubleshoot Sound Problems
Check if audio works with headphones (tests if speakers are the issue)
Restart Windows Audio service (see below)

children.name: Restart Audio Service
children.command:
net stop audiosrv
net start audiosrv
children.description: Restarts the Windows Audio service. Fixes many cases of sudden audio loss without requiring a full restart.

children.name: Reinstall Audio Driver
children.description: Corrupted or incompatible audio drivers are a common cause of no sound or distorted audio in Windows.
steps: Open devmgmt.msc
Expand 'Sound, video and game controllers'
Right-click your audio device → Uninstall device → check 'Delete the driver software'
Restart the computer — Windows will auto-reinstall the driver
If the auto-installed driver doesn't work: download from your PC manufacturer's website

children.name: Audio Keeps Cutting Out
children.description: Intermittent audio dropouts are often caused by power management settings or driver issues.
steps: Device Manager → Audio device → Properties → Power Management → uncheck 'Allow computer to turn off this device'
Settings → Sound → scroll down → 'More sound settings' → Playback tab → right-click device → Properties → Advanced → uncheck 'Allow applications to take exclusive control'
Update audio driver from manufacturer website

children.name: Microphone Not Working
children.description: Microphone detection failures — check privacy settings first.
steps: Settings → Privacy & Security → Microphone → ensure app access is On
Right-click speaker icon → Sound Settings → scroll to Input → select correct microphone
Check if mic is muted in hardware (physical mute button or switch)
Device Manager → Audio → right-click microphone device → Enable Device
Run: ms-settings:privacy-microphone in Run dialog to check permissions

children.name: Display & Graphics
children.description: Fixing screen flickering, black screens, resolution problems, GPU driver issues, and monitor detection failures.

children.name: Screen Flickering
children.description: Screen flickering in Windows is usually caused by incompatible display drivers or a problematic application.
steps: Open Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc) — if the taskbar flickers but Task Manager doesn't: the issue is a program. If everything flickers: it's a driver.
For driver issue: update or roll back display driver in Device Manager
For application issue: uninstall recently installed apps
Check refresh rate: Settings → Display → Advanced display → choose highest supported rate
If using dual monitors: check if both cables are fully seated

children.name: Black Screen on Boot
children.description: A black screen after boot usually means Windows loaded but the display driver or Explorer failed to initialize.
steps: Press Ctrl+Alt+Del — if that works, open Task Manager
In Task Manager → File → Run new task → type explorer.exe
If above doesn't work: boot into Safe Mode and roll back display driver
Disable Fast Startup: Settings → Power → Additional power settings → Choose what power buttons do → uncheck 'Turn on fast startup'
If persistent: boot from USB → Repair → SFC/DISM

children.name: GPU Driver Issues
children.description: Updating, rolling back, or clean-installing GPU drivers.
steps: Download DDU (Display Driver Uninstaller) — safest driver removal tool
Boot into Safe Mode
Run DDU → Clean and Restart
Download the latest GPU driver from NVIDIA.com, AMD.com, or Intel.com
Install the fresh driver after DDU cleanup

children.name: Monitor Not Detected
children.description: Second monitor not showing up in display settings.
steps: Settings → Display → scroll down → 'Detect' button
Try a different cable (HDMI, DisplayPort, USB-C)
Try the monitor on a different port on the GPU
Update GPU driver
Right-click desktop → Display settings → confirm 'Multiple displays' setting

children.name: Resolution Won't Change
children.description: Stuck at wrong resolution, usually caused by a missing or generic display driver.
steps: Right-click desktop → Display settings → Display resolution → select correct resolution
If correct resolution isn't listed: GPU driver is not installed properly
Device Manager → Display adapters → check if it says 'Microsoft Basic Display Adapter'
If Basic Display Adapter: reinstall GPU driver from manufacturer

children.name: Printer Issues
children.description: Fixing printers that won't print, aren't detected, are offline, or have stuck print queues.

children.name: Printer Offline Fix
children.description: Printer shows as Offline even when it's on and connected.
steps: Settings → Bluetooth & devices → Printers & scanners → select printer → Open print queue
Printer menu → uncheck 'Use Printer Offline'
Turn printer off, wait 30 seconds, turn back on
If wireless: reconnect printer to Wi-Fi
Delete and re-add the printer

children.name: Clear Print Queue (Stuck Jobs)
children.description: Stuck print jobs block all new printing. Clear the queue manually by stopping the Print Spooler service.
children.command:
net stop spooler
del /Q /F /S "%systemroot%\System32\spool\PRINTERS\*.*"
net start spooler
steps: Open Admin CMD
Run: net stop spooler
Run: del /Q /F /S "%systemroot%\System32\spool\PRINTERS\*.*"
Run: net start spooler
Return to printer and retry

children.name: Reinstall Printer Driver
children.description: Corrupted printer drivers cause most persistent printer failures.
steps: Settings → Bluetooth & devices → Printers & scanners → select printer → Remove device
devmgmt.msc → View → Show hidden devices → Printers → uninstall old drivers
Download fresh driver from printer manufacturer's website
Install driver, then re-add the printer

children.name: Print Spooler Service
children.description: The Print Spooler manages all print jobs. If it's stopped or crashed, no printing is possible.
steps: Open services.msc
Find 'Print Spooler' in the list
Right-click → Restart
If Startup Type is not 'Automatic', double-click → change to Automatic → click Start

children.name: Performance (Slow PC)
children.description: Diagnosing and fixing a slow Windows computer — from startup times to high CPU/RAM/disk usage.

children.name: Check Resource Usage
children.description: Identify what's consuming CPU, RAM, or Disk.
steps: Open Task Manager → Processes tab
Click CPU, Memory, or Disk column headers to sort by usage
Identify processes using >50% of any resource
Right-click → Search online to identify unfamiliar processes
For persistent monitoring: use Resource Monitor (perfmon /res)

children.name: Disable Startup Programs
children.description: Too many startup programs slow boot time. Disable non-essential ones.
steps: Task Manager → Startup apps tab
Right-click programs you don't need immediately at boot → Disable
Focus on disabling: update helpers, manufacturer utilities, chat apps
Do NOT disable: antivirus, audio drivers, GPU software

children.name: PC Performance Score
children.description: Runs the Windows System Assessment Tool and returns your PC's performance score across CPU, memory, disk, and graphics subsystems. Run in PowerShell as Administrator.

children.name: Reliability Monitor
children.description: Opens Windows Reliability Monitor — a graphical timeline of system stability events, crashes, errors, and warnings. Excellent for identifying what caused a system to become unstable.

children.name: Disk Cleanup
children.description: Automated disk cleanup that removes common temporary files without user interaction. For more control: run cleanmgr and manually select file categories including 'System files'.

children.name: Adjust Visual Effects
children.description: Windows visual effects consume RAM and GPU resources. Disabling them speeds up older systems significantly.
steps: Open sysdm.cpl → Advanced tab → Performance Settings
Select 'Adjust for best performance' to disable all effects
Or: select 'Custom' and keep only 'Show thumbnails instead of icons'
Click Apply and OK

children.name: Check Disk Health
children.description: A failing or fragmented hard drive causes extreme slowness. Run chkdsk to find and fix disk errors. Also check drive health in CrystalDiskInfo (free tool) — look for 'Good' status. Caution/Bad means the drive needs to be replaced immediately.
children.warning: Back up important data before running chkdsk /r — it scans bad sectors.

children.name: Disk Management
children.description: Tools for checking disk health, repairing file system errors, and managing drive space in Windows.

children.name: chkdsk
children.description: Check Disk scans and repairs file system errors and bad sectors.

children.name: chkdsk /f (Quick)
children.description: Scans C: drive and fixes file system errors. If the drive is in use, Windows will schedule it for the next restart.

children.name: chkdsk /f /r /x (Full)
children.description: Full scan: fixes errors (/f), locates bad sectors and recovers readable data (/r), forces dismount before check (/x).
children.warning: Back up data before running. Never cancel mid-scan.

children.name: Disk Cleanup (cleanmgr)
children.description: Windows built-in temp file removal utility.

children.name: cleanmgr (GUI)
children.description: Launches the graphical Disk Cleanup tool.

children.name: cleanmgr /verylowdisk
children.description: Automated cleanup of common temp files with no UI interaction.

children.name: Export Drivers Before Reinstall
children.description: Exports all currently installed drivers to a folder before reinstalling Windows so you don't have to hunt for them afterward.

children.name: Windows Updates
children.description: Fixing Windows Update failures — from corrupt downloads to stuck installs and specific KB error codes.

children.name: Standard Repair Protocol
children.description: Run in Admin CMD. Wait for each command to complete before starting the next. Then restart. This fixes the majority of update failures.

children.name: Reset Windows Update Components
children.description: Manually resets all Windows Update services and caches — the nuclear option for stubborn update failures.
children.command:
net stop wuauserv
net stop cryptSvc
net stop bits
net stop msiserver
ren C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution SoftwareDistribution.old
ren C:\Windows\System32\catroot2 catroot2.old
net start wuauserv
net start cryptSvc
net start bits
net start msiserver
children.warning: Run each command individually in Admin CMD in the order shown.

children.name: Configure Update Services
children.description: Ensure these services are running and set to Automatic: App Readiness, Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS), Windows Update. Open services.msc, double-click each, set Startup Type to Automatic, click Start.

children.name: winver (Check Version)
children.description: Displays your Windows version (e.g. 23H2, 24H2) and build number. Needed to download the correct manual patch from the Update Catalog.

children.name: Manual Patch via Update Catalog
children.description: Download and install a specific KB update manually when Windows Update fails to deliver it automatically.
steps: Run winver to note your Windows version
Settings → System → About → note System type (64-bit)
Visit: catalog.update.microsoft.com
Search for the KB number (e.g. KB5079473)
Download the .msu file matching your version and architecture
Run the .msu file and restart

children.name: Update Error Codes
children.description: Specific Windows Update error codes and their fixes. If standard repair (sfc/DISM) doesn't resolve, try the targeted fix below for the exact code shown.

children.name: Error 0x80070002
children.description: Windows Update can't find a file it needs. Usually caused by a corrupted SoftwareDistribution folder. Standard fix: stop Windows Update services, rename SoftwareDistribution, restart services.
children.command:
net stop wuauserv
net stop bits
ren C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution SoftwareDistribution.old
net start wuauserv
net start bits
steps: Open Admin CMD
Run the commands above, in order
Open Settings → Windows Update → 'Check for updates' — Windows will rebuild SoftwareDistribution and re-download updates

children.name: Error 0x800f0922
children.description: Update failed to connect to the update server OR a previous .NET Framework installation failed. Often caused by a corrupted scheduled task or insufficient space on the System Reserved partition. Microsoft's KB documents a specific scheduled-task fix.
steps: Check VPN: disconnect any active VPN, then retry update — VPNs commonly cause 0x800f0922
Check System Reserved partition size: needs at least 500 MB free — use Disk Management to check
If scheduled-task related (per Microsoft KB): delete the corrupted StartComponentCleanup task with the command shown, then re-create it via Task Scheduler import
Disable third-party antivirus temporarily and retry

children.name: Error 0x80073712
children.description: A file needed by Windows Update is missing or corrupted. Typically a CBS (Component-Based Servicing) manifest issue. Standard fix is DISM RestoreHealth followed by SFC.
steps: Open Admin CMD
Run: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth (may take 30+ minutes)
When DISM completes successfully, run: sfc /scannow
Restart and retry Windows Update
If DISM fails with the same error: use the offline ISO source method (see DISM section)

children.name: Error 0x80070005 (Access Denied)
children.description: Windows Update or activation got 'Access denied'. Caused by insufficient permissions on the SoftwareDistribution folder, corrupted update components, or running under a non-admin user.
children.command:
net stop wuauserv
net stop cryptSvc
net stop bits
net stop msiserver
ren C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution SoftwareDistribution.old
ren C:\Windows\System32\catroot2 catroot2.old
net start wuauserv
net start cryptSvc
net start bits
net start msiserver
steps: Verify you're signed in as an administrator
Run the full Windows Update component reset (above commands, in order, as Admin)
Verify date and time are correct: Settings → Time & language → 'Set time automatically' On
Run the Windows Update troubleshooter: Settings → System → Troubleshoot → Other troubleshooters → Windows Update → Run

children.name: Boot & Startup Issues
children.description: Fixing computers that fail to boot, get stuck in loops, show the SrtTrail.txt error, or display boot configuration errors.

children.name: SrtTrail.txt Error
children.description: This error appears when Automatic Repair fails. Boot from a Windows USB → Repair → Troubleshoot → Advanced Options → Command Prompt.

children.name: Check Disk from Recovery
children.description: Run from Recovery CMD after booting from Windows USB. Finds and repairs disk errors causing boot failures.
children.warning: Do NOT cancel mid-scan. Replace C: with your actual Windows drive letter.

children.name: bootrec /fixmbr
children.description: Repairs the Master Boot Record. Run from Recovery CMD.

children.name: bootrec /fixboot
children.description: Writes a new boot sector to the system partition. Run from Recovery CMD.

children.name: bootrec /rebuildbcd
children.description: Rebuilds the Boot Configuration Data store. The most powerful bootrec command — fixes most 'Windows failed to start' errors. Run from Recovery CMD.

children.name: Offline DISM Repair
children.description: For when Windows won't boot at all. Run from USB Recovery CMD. CRITICAL: Use /Image: not /Online. Your broken Windows may be on D: not C: in Recovery — type 'dir c:' and 'dir d:' to find which has the Windows folder.
children.warning: Replace D: with your actual broken Windows drive, F: with your ISO drive.

children.name: Offline SFC
children.description: Standard sfc /scannow fails when run offline. Use this version with explicit path flags from Recovery CMD.

children.name: Create Local Account (During Setup)
children.description: During Windows 11 setup when asked to sign into Microsoft account, press Shift+F10 (or Fn+Shift+F10 on laptops) to open CMD. Run this command to bypass Microsoft account requirement and create a local account instead. Set username to 'Owner', leave Password blank.
children.warning: On laptops, you may need Fn+Shift+F10 to activate the F10 key.

children.name: Startup Repair (GUI)
children.description: Windows built-in Startup Repair tool.
steps: Boot from Windows USB drive
Click 'Repair your computer' (NOT Install Now)
Troubleshoot → Advanced Options → Startup Repair
Select your Windows installation and let it run
If Startup Repair fails, use the bootrec or DISM commands above

children.name: Driver Issues
children.description: Installing, updating, rolling back, and removing device drivers that cause system instability, hardware failure, or BSODs.

children.name: Update All Drivers
children.description: Open Device Manager and look for any device with a yellow warning triangle (!) — these have driver problems. Right-click → Update driver. For critical hardware (GPU, network), always download drivers directly from the manufacturer's website rather than using Windows Update.

children.name: Roll Back a Driver
children.description: If a problem started after a driver update, roll back to the previous version.
steps: devmgmt.msc → find the device
Right-click → Properties → Driver tab
Click 'Roll Back Driver' (available only if a previous driver was installed)
Select the reason and click Yes
Restart the computer

children.name: List All Drivers
children.description: Lists every driver installed on the system with verbose details. Pipe to clip to copy the full list to clipboard.

children.name: Export Drivers Backup
children.description: Exports all drivers to C:\DriversBackup before a Windows reinstall, so you can restore them without internet access afterward.

children.name: Security & Malware
children.description: Scanning for malware, using Windows Defender, checking for suspicious processes, and recovering from infections.

children.name: Windows Defender Full Scan
children.description: Runs a full Windows Defender antivirus scan from the command line. ScanType 2 = Full Scan. ScanType 1 = Quick Scan. Must run as Admin.

children.name: Update Defender Signatures
children.description: Forces Windows Defender to download the latest malware definition signatures. Run before a scan for best results.

children.name: Check Suspicious Processes
children.description: Lists all running processes with verbose info. Look for unfamiliar process names, processes running from temp folders (C:\Users\...\AppData\Temp\), or processes consuming unusual resources.

children.name: Check Startup Items for Malware
children.description: Open msconfig → Startup tab. Any startup item pointing to a temp folder, AppData\Roaming, or an unusual path is suspicious. Also use: Task Manager → Startup apps for the modern view.

children.name: Reset Browser (Post-Infection)
children.description: After removing malware, reset browsers to remove hijacked settings, extensions, and modified search engines.
steps: Chrome: Settings → Reset settings → Restore settings to original defaults
Edge: Settings → Reset settings → Restore settings to default values
Firefox: Help → More Troubleshooting Info → Refresh Firefox
After reset: check and re-install only trusted extensions

children.name: USB & Peripherals
children.description: Troubleshooting USB ports not working, devices not recognized, and peripheral connection issues.

children.name: USB Device Not Recognized
children.description: USB device shows 'Unknown device' or isn't detected at all.
steps: Try the device in a different USB port
Try a different USB cable
devmgmt.msc → View → Show hidden devices → look for Unknown Device with !
Right-click → Update driver or Uninstall and reconnect
Device Manager → Universal Serial Bus controllers → right-click each USB Root Hub → Properties → Power Management → uncheck 'Allow computer to turn off this device'
Disable USB Selective Suspend: Control Panel → Power Options → Change plan settings → Change advanced power settings → USB settings → Selective suspend → Disabled

children.name: Reset USB Controllers
children.description: Sometimes USB controllers get into a bad state. Uninstall all USB Root Hubs in Device Manager → Universal Serial Bus controllers → restart the computer. Windows will reinstall them automatically.

children.name: Keyboard/Mouse Not Working
children.description: Keyboard or mouse stops responding or is intermittent.
steps: Try a different USB port
For wireless: replace batteries, re-pair the device
Check device in Device Manager for driver errors
Try the device on another computer to rule out hardware failure
For keyboard: if only some keys fail — clean keyboard or check for stuck keys

children.name: File Explorer Issues
children.description: Fixing File Explorer crashes, freezes, slow loading, and thumbnail cache corruption.

children.name: Restart File Explorer
children.description: Kills and restarts the File Explorer process without rebooting. Fixes most temporary Explorer freezes, crashes, or UI glitches instantly.

children.name: Clear Thumbnail Cache
children.description: Corrupted thumbnail cache causes Explorer to crash or show blank thumbnails. Clears all cache files and restarts Explorer.

children.name: Reset File Explorer Options
children.description: Opens Folder Options to reset Explorer view settings to default. Useful when Explorer behaves unexpectedly with hidden files or folder views.

children.name: Power Management
children.description: Managing sleep, hibernate, power plans, and diagnosing power-related performance and battery issues.

children.name: powercfg /energy
children.description: Analyzes the system for 60 seconds and generates a detailed HTML report highlighting power efficiency problems and battery drain causes.

children.name: powercfg /batteryreport
children.description: Generates a detailed HTML battery health report showing capacity history, charge cycles, and estimated battery life. Saved to the current directory.

children.name: Disable Fast Startup
children.description: Disables Hibernate and Fast Startup — which cause issues like black screens, devices not waking properly, and USB problems. Run as Admin. This is often a required troubleshooting step.

children.name: Set High Performance Mode
children.description: Activates the High Performance power plan. Prevents the CPU from throttling and ensures maximum performance at all times. Use on desktops or when plugged in. To restore Balanced: use GUID 381b4222-f694-41f0-9685-ff5bb260df2e

children.name: Process & System Commands
children.description: Essential Windows command-line tools for process management, system information, and administrative tasks.

children.name: systeminfo
children.description: Displays comprehensive system information: OS version, hotfixes installed, RAM, processor, BIOS version, network adapters, and more.

children.name: whoami
children.description: Displays the current user and domain. Useful when troubleshooting permission issues.

children.name: tasklist /v
children.description: Lists all running processes with verbose details: user, CPU time, memory usage.

children.name: taskkill /IM
children.description: Terminates a process by its .exe name. Replace notepad.exe with your target process name from tasklist.

children.name: taskkill /PID
children.description: Force-terminates a process by its Process ID. Find the PID in tasklist /v output. /F forces termination of stubborn processes.

children.name: shutdown Commands
children.description: Commands for restarting, shutting down, and cancelling pending shutdowns from the command line.

children.name: shutdown /r (Restart)
children.description: Immediately restarts the computer. /t 0 means 0 second delay.

children.name: shutdown /s (Shutdown)
children.description: Immediately shuts down the computer.

children.name: shutdown /a (Abort)
children.description: Cancels a pending shutdown or restart.

children.name: driverquery /v
children.description: Lists all installed drivers verbosely and copies to clipboard.

children.name: Mac
children.description: Troubleshooting tools, Terminal commands, and step-by-step solutions for macOS issues on both Intel and Apple Silicon Macs.

children.name: Startup Issues
children.description: Fixing Macs that won't turn on, get stuck on the Apple logo, show a question mark folder, or boot to a black screen.

children.name: Mac Won't Turn On
children.description: Basic power troubleshooting when the Mac shows no signs of life.
steps: Ensure the power cable is securely connected and the outlet works
For MacBook: connect charger and wait 10 minutes before pressing power
Try a different charger or power adapter
Reset SMC (System Management Controller) — see SMC Reset section
For desktop Mac: unplug power cord, wait 15 seconds, replug and power on
If still no response: the logic board may need service

children.name: Stuck on Apple Logo
children.description: Mac boots to the Apple logo and loading bar but never reaches the desktop.
steps: Force restart: hold Power button 10 seconds until it shuts off, then restart
Boot into Safe Mode (see Safe Mode section) — if it boots in Safe Mode, a login item is the cause
Boot into Recovery Mode and run First Aid in Disk Utility
Reinstall macOS from Recovery Mode (does not erase your data)

children.name: Question Mark Folder (?)
children.description: A blinking folder with a question mark means the Mac cannot find a valid startup disk. Usually caused by a disconnected or failed drive, or corrupted startup disk settings.
steps: Boot into Recovery Mode
Open Startup Disk (System Preferences) — select your Macintosh HD
If startup disk isn't listed: open Disk Utility → select Macintosh HD → First Aid
If First Aid finds errors it can't fix: reinstall macOS or replace drive

children.name: Boot into Recovery Mode
children.description: Recovery Mode provides access to Disk Utility, Terminal, and macOS reinstallation tools without booting into macOS.
steps: Intel Mac: Restart → immediately hold Command + R until Apple logo appears
Apple Silicon Mac: Press and hold Power button → 'Loading startup options' → click Options → Continue
From Recovery: use Disk Utility, reinstall macOS, or open Terminal

children.name: Boot into Safe Mode
children.description: Safe Mode loads only essential system software, disabling all login items and third-party extensions. If the Mac works in Safe Mode, a startup item or extension is the cause of the problem.
steps: Intel Mac: Restart → hold Shift immediately → release when login screen appears
Apple Silicon Mac: Shut down → press and hold Power button until 'Loading startup options' → select drive → hold Shift → click 'Continue in Safe Mode'
Safe Mode indicator: 'Safe Boot' appears in red text at top-right of login screen
To exit Safe Mode: restart normally (no keys held)

children.name: Startup Disk Full (Boot Failure)
children.description: If the startup disk is completely full, macOS may fail to boot.
steps: Boot into Recovery Mode
Open Terminal from Recovery
Type: ls /Volumes/ to see drive names
Navigate to large folders: cd /Volumes/Macintosh\ HD/private/var/folders
Delete specific large log or cache files
Alternatively: use a bootable USB with a tool like DiskDiag

children.name: Bluetooth Mouse/Keyboard Not Working in Recovery
children.description: Bluetooth peripherals (Magic Mouse/Trackpad/Keyboard) often don't connect during macOS Recovery Mode because the Bluetooth stack isn't fully loaded. You need a wired (USB) keyboard/mouse to perform Recovery operations on Apple Silicon Macs.
steps: Connect a USB or USB-C wired keyboard and mouse before entering Recovery Mode
If you only have wireless: on Magic Keyboard/Mouse, connect via Lightning/USB-C cable — it acts as wired in Recovery
Apple Silicon Macs: power down fully, then hold the power button until 'Loading startup options' appears — wait an extra 15 seconds with wired input plugged in
If a wired keyboard still doesn't work, the Recovery partition itself may be damaged — boot to Internet Recovery (Cmd+Option+R on Intel) or DFU restore (Apple Silicon)

children.name: Performance Issues
children.description: Diagnosing and fixing a slow Mac — spinning beach balls, high CPU/RAM usage, and sluggish applications.

children.name: Spinning Beach Ball (Frozen App)
children.description: The spinning beach ball (SPOD) indicates an application is not responding. Force-quit it to restore responsiveness.
steps: Press Command + Option + Escape → select the frozen app → Force Quit
Or: right-click the app in Dock → hold Option → Force Quit appears
Or via Terminal: run 'top' to find the process, then 'kill -9 [PID]'
If the entire system is frozen: hold Power button 10 seconds to force restart

children.name: Activity Monitor
children.description: macOS equivalent of Windows Task Manager. Shows all running processes and their resource usage.
steps: Finder → Applications → Utilities → Activity Monitor
Or: Spotlight (Command + Space) → type 'Activity Monitor'
Click CPU, Memory, Energy, or Disk tabs to sort by usage
Select a resource-hogging process → click X button to quit it

children.name: Free Up RAM
children.description: Forces macOS to purge inactive memory (RAM cache). Temporarily frees memory that macOS was holding in reserve. Run in Terminal. Note: this is usually not necessary — macOS manages memory efficiently.

children.name: Check Disk Space
children.description: Shows disk space usage for all mounted drives in human-readable format. Low disk space (<10% free) significantly degrades performance on all Macs, especially those with SSDs.

children.name: Manage Login Items (Slow Boot)
children.description: Too many startup apps slow Mac boot time.
steps: Apple menu → System Settings → General → Login Items
Toggle off apps you don't need at startup
Also remove Launch Agents from: ~/Library/LaunchAgents/

children.name: Rebuild Spotlight Index
children.description: A corrupted Spotlight index causes slow searches and high CPU usage from the mdworker process.
steps: Open Terminal
Run: sudo mdutil -E /
Enter your password
Spotlight will reindex — this may take 1-2 hours and slow the Mac temporarily

children.name: Kernel Panic
children.description: A kernel panic causes the Mac to display 'Your computer restarted because of a problem' — the macOS equivalent of a BSOD. The Mac saves a log of what caused it.

children.name: Read Kernel Panic Log
children.description: Shows kernel panic log entries from the past 24 hours in Terminal. Also check: Console app → Crash Reports → look for .panic files.

children.name: Check for Bad RAM
children.description: Faulty RAM is a very common cause of recurring kernel panics.
steps: For Intel Macs with removable RAM: reseat RAM modules (remove and reinsert)
Run Apple Diagnostics: restart and hold D (Intel) or hold Power button, then D (Apple Silicon)
Apple Diagnostics will test memory and report any errors with a code
If RAM is faulty: replace it (user-replaceable on some Mac models)

children.name: Disconnect External Devices
children.description: External devices with bad drivers or firmware can trigger kernel panics. Isolate the cause.
steps: Shut down the Mac
Disconnect ALL external devices (drives, hubs, monitors via adapters)
Boot normally — if panics stop, reconnect devices one at a time
The device that triggers a panic when reconnected is the culprit

children.name: Update macOS and Apps
children.description: Lists available macOS software updates in Terminal. Outdated macOS versions and apps are a common kernel panic cause. Install all available updates.

children.name: Run Disk First Aid
children.description: Disk corruption can trigger kernel panics. Run First Aid on the startup disk from Recovery Mode.
steps: Boot into Recovery Mode (Command+R on Intel, hold Power on Apple Silicon)
Open Disk Utility
Select 'Macintosh HD' in the left sidebar
Click First Aid → Run
If First Aid reports errors it can't fix: reinstall macOS

children.name: Reinstall macOS
children.description: If kernel panics persist after all other fixes, reinstall macOS. This does NOT erase your data — it replaces only the OS files.
steps: Boot into Recovery Mode
Select 'Reinstall macOS' from the Recovery menu
Follow the on-screen prompts
This process takes 1-2 hours depending on internet speed

children.name: Disk & Storage
children.description: Using Disk Utility, First Aid, and Terminal to check, repair, and manage storage on macOS.

children.name: Disk Utility First Aid
children.description: macOS built-in tool for checking and repairing disk errors.
steps: Finder → Applications → Utilities → Disk Utility
Select your startup disk in the left panel
Click First Aid → Run
For startup disk repair: boot from Recovery Mode first, then run First Aid

children.name: diskutil (Terminal)
children.command:
diskutil list
diskutil verifyDisk /dev/disk0
diskutil repairDisk /dev/disk0
children.description: Command-line Disk Utility. 'list' shows all disks. 'verifyDisk' checks for errors. 'repairDisk' repairs them. Replace /dev/disk0 with your disk identifier from diskutil list.

children.name: Check Disk Space Usage
children.description: df -h shows overall disk space. du -sh shows specific folder sizes. Use to find what's consuming disk space.

children.name: Free Up Startup Disk Space
children.description: When startup disk is full (common issue on Macs).
steps: Apple menu → About This Mac → More Info → Storage Settings
Click Recommendations — use built-in tools to optimize
Empty Trash: Finder → Empty Trash
Clear Downloads folder
Remove large unused apps: Finder → Applications → sort by Size
Clear browser caches
Remove old Time Machine local snapshots: tmutil deletelocalsnapshots /

children.name: Erase and Format a Drive
children.description: Erases and formats a disk with APFS filesystem. Replace 'MacintoshHD' with your desired disk name and /dev/disk2 with your disk identifier from 'diskutil list'. WARNING: This PERMANENTLY DESTROYS all data on that disk.
children.warning: DESTRUCTIVE: Back up all data before running. Cannot be undone.

children.name: 'Disk Not Ejected Properly' Loop
children.description: Repeating 'Disk Not Ejected Properly' notifications for an external drive, often after the Mac wakes from sleep. Caused by macOS putting the drive to sleep too aggressively (especially USB-C/Thunderbolt enclosures) or a faulty cable.
steps: Try a different USB-C / USB-A / Thunderbolt cable — cheap cables cause this
Disable disk sleep: System Settings → Battery (or Energy Saver) → Options → uncheck 'Put hard disks to sleep when possible'
Plug the drive directly into the Mac, not through a hub or dock
For external SSDs: check the enclosure firmware — many SanDisk/SSK enclosures had known sleep bugs
On laptops, set 'Prevent automatic sleeping on power adapter when display is off' for testing
If drive shows but Disk Utility reports errors: First Aid → if it fails, the drive may be failing
children.warning: Repeated improper ejection CAN cause file system corruption over time. Run Disk Utility First Aid if the warnings have been happening for a while.

children.name: Network Issues (Mac)
children.description: Fixing Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and internet connectivity problems on macOS using System Settings and Terminal.

children.name: Wi-Fi Won't Connect
children.description: Basic Wi-Fi troubleshooting on macOS.
steps: Turn Wi-Fi off and on again in menu bar or System Settings
Forget the network: System Settings → Wi-Fi → Details → Forget This Network → reconnect
Restart router (unplug 30 seconds)
Check if other devices connect to the same network
Flush DNS cache (see DNS section)
Delete Wi-Fi preference files (see below)

children.name: Delete Wi-Fi Preference Files
children.command:
sudo rm /Library/Preferences/SystemConfiguration/com.apple.airport.preferences.plist
sudo rm /Library/Preferences/SystemConfiguration/com.apple.network.identification.plist
sudo rm /Library/Preferences/SystemConfiguration/NetworkInterfaces.plist
children.description: Removes corrupted Wi-Fi configuration files. macOS will recreate them on restart. This fixes persistent Wi-Fi authentication failures.
children.warning: Restart the Mac after deleting these files.

children.name: Flush DNS Cache (Mac)
children.description: Clears the DNS cache on macOS. The command varies by macOS version. This version works on macOS Monterey, Ventura, Sonoma, and Sequoia.

children.name: Renew DHCP Lease
children.description: Forces macOS to request a new IP address from the router.
steps: System Settings → Network → select your Wi-Fi or Ethernet connection
Click Details → TCP/IP tab
Click 'Renew DHCP Lease'

children.name: Network Diagnostics
children.description: Built-in macOS network quality test (macOS Monterey+). Tests upload speed, download speed, and network responsiveness. Run in Terminal.

children.name: Bluetooth Issues
children.description: Bluetooth devices not pairing, disconnecting, or not found.
steps: Toggle Bluetooth off and on in menu bar
Remove and re-pair the device: System Settings → Bluetooth → click X next to device → Forget → re-pair
Reset Bluetooth module (Intel Mac): hold Shift+Option and click Bluetooth menu bar icon → Reset Bluetooth Module → Yes
Apple Silicon Mac: delete Bluetooth preferences file below and restart

children.name: SMC Reset
children.description: The System Management Controller (SMC) manages low-level functions: power, battery, fans, sleep, and LED indicators. Reset when experiencing: fans running at max speed, not sleeping properly, battery not charging, power button not responding, or display backlight issues.

children.name: MacBook with T2 Chip (2018-2020)
children.description: For Intel MacBooks with Apple T2 security chip (MacBook Pro 2018+, MacBook Air 2018+).
steps: Shut down the Mac
Hold: Right Shift + Left Option + Left Control for 7 seconds
Continue holding those keys while also pressing the Power button for another 7 seconds
Release all keys, wait a few seconds, then press Power to turn on

children.name: MacBook without T2 Chip (2017 and earlier)
children.description: For older Intel MacBooks without the T2 security chip.
steps: Shut down the Mac
Connect the MagSafe/USB-C charger
Hold: Left Shift + Left Control + Left Option + Power button for 10 seconds
Release all keys simultaneously
Press Power to turn on

children.name: Mac Mini, Mac Pro, iMac (Intel)
children.description: SMC reset for Intel desktop Macs.
steps: Shut down the Mac
Unplug the power cord and wait 15 seconds
Plug the power cord back in and wait 5 seconds
Press the Power button to turn on

children.name: Apple Silicon Macs (M1/M2/M3/M4)
children.description: Apple Silicon Macs (M-series chips) do not have an SMC. Instead, restart the Mac — this performs the equivalent function. For persistent issues, shut down, wait 30 seconds, and power on.
steps: Apple menu → Shut Down
Wait 30 seconds
Press Power button to restart

children.name: NVRAM / PRAM Reset
children.description: NVRAM (Non-Volatile RAM) stores settings like display resolution, time zone, startup disk, and sound volume. Reset when experiencing: wrong time zone, wrong startup disk selected, wrong screen resolution, kernel panics.

children.name: Intel Mac NVRAM Reset
children.description: Works on all Intel-based Macs. Apple Silicon Macs manage NVRAM automatically — a separate reset is not necessary.
steps: Shut down the Mac
Press Power button, then immediately hold Command + Option + P + R
Hold for about 20 seconds — on older Macs you'll hear the startup chime twice
Release the keys and let the Mac finish starting up
Reconfigure: time zone, display resolution, startup disk in System Settings

children.name: Apple Silicon NVRAM
children.description: Apple Silicon Macs reset NVRAM automatically during every restart. No manual reset key combination is needed or available.

children.name: Audio Issues (Mac)
children.description: Fixing no sound, distorted audio, and sound output/input problems on macOS.

children.name: No Sound (Basic Checks)
children.description: Initial sound output checks on macOS.
steps: Click Apple menu → System Settings → Sound
Ensure the correct output device is selected and volume is up
Option + click the volume slider in menu bar to see all output devices
Check if a Bluetooth device is stealing the audio output
Restart coreaudiod (see below)

children.name: Restart Core Audio
children.description: Kills the Core Audio daemon and restarts it automatically. Fixes most cases of sudden audio loss on macOS without requiring a restart.

children.name: Reset Sound Preferences
children.description: Deletes corrupted sound preference files. macOS will recreate them with defaults on next restart. Fixes persistent sound output/input configuration issues.
children.warning: Restart the Mac after deleting these files.

children.name: Display Issues (Mac)
children.description: Fixing resolution problems, external monitor detection, and screen flickering on macOS.

children.name: External Monitor Not Detected
children.description: Steps to diagnose when an external display isn't recognized by macOS.
steps: System Settings → Displays → click 'Detect Displays' button
Try a different cable (HDMI, DisplayPort, USB-C)
Try a different port on the Mac
For Apple Silicon: some ports share bandwidth — try the other USB-C port
Restart the Mac with the monitor connected

children.name: Wrong Resolution
children.command: System Settings → Displays → Resolution → select 'Scaled' → choose correct resolution
children.description: If the display shows a 'Looks like' resolution and the correct resolution isn't available, the display driver or cable may be limiting the signal.

children.name: Screen Flickering (Mac)
children.description: Steps to address screen flicker on macOS.
steps: System Settings → Accessibility → Display → uncheck 'Reduce motion'
Try a different cable or adapter — cheap HDMI adapters cause flickering
Reset NVRAM (Intel Mac) — see NVRAM Reset section
Check Activity Monitor for GPU-heavy processes
Update macOS — display flickering bugs are often fixed in updates

children.name: Battery & Power (Mac)
children.description: Diagnosing battery health, charging issues, and power consumption problems on MacBooks.

children.name: Check Battery Health
children.description: Shows detailed battery information including cycle count, condition (Normal/Service Recommended), and charging status. A battery with >1000 cycles or 'Service Recommended' condition needs replacing.

children.name: Battery Not Charging
children.description: Steps to diagnose a MacBook that won't charge.
steps: Try a different USB-C cable and charger
Clean the USB-C port gently with compressed air
Reset SMC (see SMC Reset section)
Check System Settings → Battery — if it shows 'Not Charging' intentionally, turn off Optimized Battery Charging
Check for heat — MacBooks won't charge above 95% when very hot

children.name: Check What's Draining Battery
children.description: Identify which apps are using the most battery.
steps: Click Battery icon in menu bar — see which apps are using 'significant energy'
Activity Monitor → Energy tab → sort by Energy Impact
System Settings → Battery → Battery Health → Manage

children.name: Generate Diagnostics Report
children.description: Generates a comprehensive diagnostic report including system logs, crash reports, hardware info, and battery data. Saved to Desktop as a compressed archive. Share with Apple Support when needed.

children.name: App Issues (Mac)
children.description: Fixing application crashes, 'App is damaged' errors, apps not opening, and Mac App Store problems.

children.name: Force Quit an App
children.description: Opens the Force Quit dialog to close unresponsive apps. Select the frozen app and click Force Quit.

children.name: App Won't Open (Gatekeeper)
children.description: macOS Gatekeeper blocks apps not from the App Store or identified developers. This command removes the quarantine attribute from a specific app. Replace 'AppName.app' with your app's actual name.
children.warning: Only run this for apps you trust. Quarantine protects against malware.

children.name: Clear App Cache
children.description: Clears the cache for a specific application. Navigate to ~/Library/Caches/ in Finder (hold Option, click Go menu → Library) to find your app's cache folder name.

children.name: Reinstall an App
children.description: Clean reinstall steps for a misbehaving app.
steps: Drag the app from Applications folder to Trash
Use a tool like AppCleaner (free) to also remove all preference files
Empty Trash
Reinstall from App Store or developer website

children.name: App Store Not Loading
steps: Force-quit App Store: Command+Option+Escape → App Store → Force Quit
Clear App Store cache: open Terminal → type: rm -rf ~/Library/Caches/com.apple.appstore
Sign out: App Store → [your name] → Sign Out → sign back in
Check date and time — wrong system clock breaks App Store authentication
children.description: Mac App Store stuck loading, blank, or won't authenticate. Force-quit and clear cache.

children.name: Permissions & Maintenance
children.description: Repairing disk permissions, running maintenance scripts, and system-level macOS housekeeping.

children.name: Run Maintenance Scripts
children.description: macOS has built-in maintenance scripts (daily, weekly, monthly) that usually run automatically. Force-run all three manually if the Mac is slow or hasn't been on during their scheduled time (3am).

children.name: Repair Disk Permissions (Disk Utility)
children.description: In older macOS versions (pre-El Capitan), you could repair disk permissions in Disk Utility. In modern macOS, SIP (System Integrity Protection) handles this automatically. Run First Aid in Disk Utility instead.

children.name: Clear User Caches
children.description: Clears all user-level application caches. Safe to run — apps will rebuild their caches. Can free significant disk space and resolve app misbehavior.
children.warning: Apps may start slower once after this as they rebuild caches.

children.name: Reset Launchpad
children.command: defaults write com.apple.dock ResetLaunchpad -bool true; killall Dock
children.description: Resets Launchpad to its default layout — useful if app icons are missing, duplicated, or in the wrong order.

children.name: Terminal Utilities
children.description: Useful macOS Terminal commands for diagnostics, system info, and helpful built-in tools.

children.name: System Diagnostics
children.description: Generates a comprehensive diagnostic report (logs, crash reports, hardware info) saved to Desktop. Share with Apple Support.

children.name: Software Updates (Terminal)
children.description: Lists available updates (--list) and installs all of them (--all --install --force). Useful when the GUI Software Update is broken.

children.name: Check Uptime
children.description: Shows how long the Mac has been running since last restart. Long uptimes can contribute to performance degradation.

children.name: Check macOS Version
children.description: Displays the macOS version, build number, and product name from the Terminal.

children.name: Weather in Terminal
children.description: Displays a 3-day weather forecast in the Terminal. Also works: curl wttr.in/moon for the current moon phase.

children.name: Watch Star Wars (ASCII)
children.description: Watch Star Wars Episode IV in ASCII art via netcat. Press Ctrl+C to exit.

children.name: Browser Issues
children.description: Fixing common problems in Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Firefox, and Safari — from slow performance and cache errors to sync, reset, and load failures.

children.name: Chrome
children.description: Google Chrome troubleshooting on Windows and Mac.

children.name: Slow / High Memory Use (Memory Saver)
children.description: Chrome's Memory Saver deactivates inactive tabs to reduce RAM usage. Turn it on for systems with limited memory or many open tabs. Optionally allow specific sites to stay active.
steps: Open Chrome → top-right ⋮ menu → Settings
On the left, select Performance
Turn on Memory Saver
To keep specific sites active: under 'Always keep these sites active', click Add and enter the site URL

children.name: ERR_CACHE_MISS
children.description: Chrome shows ERR_CACHE_MISS when it needs to re-request page content but the cache is missing or corrupted. Usually happens after submitting a form or clicking Back. Most cases resolve by reloading, clearing cache, or disabling extensions.
steps: Press Ctrl+F5 (Cmd+Shift+R on Mac) to hard-reload bypassing cache
Clear browsing data: ⋮ → Delete browsing data → Time range: All time → check 'Cached images and files' → Delete data
Try the page in Incognito (Ctrl+Shift+N) to test without extensions
If only one site is affected, the issue is likely the site's form handling — try a different browser

children.name: Sync Paused / Not Syncing
children.description: Chrome pauses sync when you sign out of any Google service (like Gmail). Click 'Verify it's you' to sign back in and resume sync. If sync turns off every time Chrome closes, enable on-device site data.
steps: If the avatar says 'Paused': click it → 'Verify it's you' → 'Sign in again'
To keep sync persistent: Settings → Privacy and security → Site Settings → Additional content settings → On-device site data → 'Allow sites to save data on your device'

children.name: Reset Chrome to Defaults
children.description: Restores Chrome to factory settings — resets default search engine, homepage, startup tab, pinned tabs, and disables extensions. Bookmarks, history, and passwords are NOT deleted. Use after an extension hijacks your browser.
steps: Open Chrome → ⋮ menu → Settings
Click 'Reset settings' in the left menu
Click 'Restore settings to their original defaults'
Click 'Reset settings' to confirm

children.name: Microsoft Edge
children.description: Edge browser troubleshooting on Windows.

children.name: Edge Won't Open / Keeps Crashing
children.description: If Edge won't open or crashes immediately on launch, the issue is usually low memory, a corrupted extension, or an outdated build. Microsoft's recommended fix sequence: close other apps, update Edge, disable extensions, then repair.
steps: Close other tabs and applications to free memory
Update Edge: ⋯ menu → Help and feedback → About Microsoft Edge
Disable extensions: edge://extensions → toggle each off
Repair Edge: Settings (Windows) → Apps → Installed apps → Microsoft Edge → ⋯ → Modify → Repair (does not delete data)

children.name: Reset Edge Settings
children.description: Resets startup page, new tab page, pinned tabs, and search engine to defaults and disables all extensions. Does NOT clear favorites, history, or saved passwords.
steps: Open Edge → ⋯ menu → Settings
Click 'Reset settings' in the left navigation
Click 'Restore settings to their default values'
Click Reset to confirm

children.name: Disable Edge Auto-Updates
children.description: Microsoft Edge auto-updates via two scheduled tasks (MicrosoftEdgeUpdateTaskMachineCore and MicrosoftEdgeUpdateTaskMachineUA) and the MicrosoftEdgeUpdate service. Disabling all three pauses automatic updates. Re-enable them to resume.
children.command:
schtasks /Change /TN "MicrosoftEdgeUpdateTaskMachineCore" /DISABLE
schtasks /Change /TN "MicrosoftEdgeUpdateTaskMachineUA" /DISABLE
sc config MicrosoftEdgeUpdate start= disabled
children.warning: Disabling updates means missing security patches. Re-enable with /ENABLE and 'start= demand' when ready.

children.name: Firefox
children.description: Mozilla Firefox troubleshooting on Windows and Mac.

children.name: Troubleshoot Mode (formerly Safe Mode)
children.description: Starts Firefox with add-ons, custom themes, and hardware acceleration disabled. If the problem disappears in Troubleshoot Mode, the cause is an extension or theme. Add-ons are kept installed but inactive.
steps: Open Firefox menu → Help → Troubleshoot Mode...
Click Restart in the confirmation dialog
Click 'Open' when prompted
Test whether the problem still occurs
Exit by restarting Firefox normally

children.name: Clear Cookies for One Site
children.description: Deletes cookies and site data for a specific website without losing your other logins. Useful when one site has stuck login or layout issues.
steps: Open Firefox menu → Settings → Privacy & Security
Scroll to 'Cookies and Site Data' → click 'Manage Data...'
In the search box, type the website name
Select the entry → click 'Remove Selected' → 'Save Changes'

children.name: Safari (Mac)
children.description: Safari troubleshooting on macOS.

children.name: Safari Won't Load Pages
children.description: When Safari shows blank pages, stops responding, or won't connect, work through Apple's recommended fix sequence: reload, update macOS, check extensions, clear cache, and verify network settings.
steps: Reload the page: View menu → Reload Page (or Cmd+R)
Force-reload bypassing cache: Cmd+Option+R
Install macOS updates: Apple menu → System Settings → General → Software Update
Disable Safari extensions: Safari → Settings → Extensions → uncheck each
Clear caches: Develop menu → Empty Caches (enable Develop menu in Settings → Advanced)
Disable iCloud Private Relay if active: System Settings → Apple Account → iCloud → Private Relay

children.name: Microsoft Office
children.description: Troubleshooting Outlook, Excel, Word, and Office activation issues. Outlook desktop client issues live here; email protocol/provider issues live in the Email Issues branch.

children.name: Outlook (Desktop)
children.description: Outlook desktop application issues — data files, offline mode, safe mode, and add-in problems.

children.name: PST File Corruption (scanpst.exe)
children.description: The Inbox Repair tool (SCANPST.EXE) scans Outlook PST data files for errors and repairs them. The tool ships with Outlook but isn't on the Start menu — you must run it from the install folder.
steps: Exit Outlook completely

Open File Explorer and navigate to your Office install folder (path varies by version):
   - Microsoft 365 / 2024 / 2021 / 2019 / 2016: C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\root\Office16\
   - Outlook 2013: C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Office\Office15\
Double-click SCANPST.EXE
Click Browse and select your .pst file (typically in C:\Users\[user]\Documents\Outlook Files\)
Click Start. If errors are found, check 'Make backup of scanned file' and click Repair
Reopen Outlook
children.warning: Run scanpst multiple times if errors persist — one pass may not catch everything. Always keep the backup file it creates.

children.name: Rebuild OST File
children.description: OST files are an offline cache of an Exchange/IMAP mailbox. If an OST is corrupted, delete it — Outlook will rebuild it automatically from the server on next launch. No data loss because the mail lives on the server.
steps: Exit Outlook
Open File Explorer → paste %localappdata%\Microsoft\Outlook into the address bar
Find the .ost file for your account and delete it (or rename to .ost.old)
Reopen Outlook — it will download a fresh copy from the server
children.warning: Only do this for Exchange/IMAP accounts where mail is on the server. For POP3 or 'local-only' folders, the OST may contain the only copy of your messages.

children.name: Outlook Stuck in Offline Mode
children.description: Outlook can get stuck showing 'Working Offline' even when connected. Toggle the Work Offline button on the Send/Receive tab to reconnect.
steps: Open Outlook → Send/Receive tab on the ribbon
Click 'Work Offline' to toggle it off — the status bar should change from 'Working Offline' to 'Connected'
If the button is greyed out: File → Account Settings → Account Settings → double-click your account → ensure server settings are correct
If still offline: restart Outlook or your computer

children.name: Open Outlook in Safe Mode
children.description: Outlook safe mode disables all add-ins. If Outlook works in safe mode, an add-in is causing the issue — disable add-ins one at a time to identify which one.
steps: Right-click Start → Run (or press Win+R)
Type: outlook.exe /safe and press Enter
If Outlook opens normally: File → Options → Add-ins → at bottom, set 'Manage' to COM Add-ins → Go → disable add-ins one at a time, restarting between each, until you find the culprit

children.name: Excel
children.description: Microsoft Excel troubleshooting.

children.name: Excel Not Responding on Open
children.description: Excel hangs, freezes, or crashes when opening files. Microsoft's recommended sequence: launch in safe mode to rule out add-ins, then update Office, then repair the install.
steps: Run excel.exe /safe (Win+R → type it). If Excel works in safe mode, an add-in is the cause.
Disable add-ins: File → Options → Add-ins → Manage: COM Add-ins → Go → uncheck all → OK
Update Office: File → Account → Update Options → Update Now
Repair Office: Settings → Apps → Installed apps → Microsoft 365 → ⋯ → Modify → Online Repair (data is not touched)

children.name: #REF! Errors After Save
children.description: The #REF! error appears when a formula references a cell that no longer exists (deleted row/column/sheet). Use Excel's Trace Precedents to find what broke; or undo immediately if it just happened.
steps: If you just made the deletion: press Ctrl+Z to undo immediately
Find the broken reference: click the #REF! cell → Formulas tab → Trace Precedents (shows arrows to the missing source)
Use Find & Replace (Ctrl+H): Find '#REF!' → Replace with a valid range, e.g. A1:A10
For pivot tables: refresh after fixing the source data range

children.name: Recover Unsaved Workbook
children.description: If AutoRecover is enabled, Excel saves versions of your workbook periodically. After a crash or accidental close-without-saving, you can recover the most recent autosave.
steps: Open Excel and create or open any workbook
Go to File → Info
Under 'Manage Workbook', look for a file labeled '(when I closed without saving)'
Click it to open, then click Restore in the yellow bar at the top to overwrite the saved version
Or: File → Open → 'Recover Unsaved Workbooks' button at the bottom of Recent files

children.name: Word
children.description: Microsoft Word troubleshooting.

children.name: Open Corrupted Word Document (Open and Repair)
children.description: Word's built-in Open and Repair recovers text from a corrupted document. Often successful when 'The file is corrupt and cannot be opened' appears.
