steps: Open Word → File → Open → Browse (do NOT use the Recent list)
Navigate to the folder containing the corrupt document
Click the file once to select it
Click the arrow next to the Open button → 'Open and Repair'

children.name: Reset Normal.dotm Template
children.description: Normal.dotm is Word's default template — it loads on every launch. If Word starts slow, opens with weird formatting, or crashes on launch, the template may be corrupted. Renaming forces Word to create a fresh default template.
steps: Close all Word windows
Press Win+R → type: %appdata%\Microsoft\Templates → Enter
Right-click Normal.dotm → Rename → change to Normal.dotm.old
Open Word — it auto-creates a new Normal.dotm with all defaults
children.warning: Any custom styles, macros, or AutoText you added to Normal.dotm will be lost. The .old file remains as a backup.

children.name: Activation & License
children.description: Office activation and product key issues.

children.name: Office Activation Error 0x80070005
children.description: Activation fails with 'Access denied' / 0x80070005. Usually caused by running as a non-admin user, antivirus blocking activation, or a previous failed activation leaving stale tokens. Microsoft's recommended fix is to run Office as Administrator and ensure your time/date are correct.
steps: Verify date and time are correct: Settings → Time & language → Date & time → 'Set time automatically' = On
Close all Office apps
Right-click any Office app shortcut (e.g. Word) → 'Run as administrator'
Sign in to activate when prompted
If still failing: run the SaRA (Support and Recovery Assistant) tool from Microsoft to auto-fix activation

children.name: Reset Office Activation (ospp.vbs)
children.description: ospp.vbs is Office's command-line activation tool. Use it to view license status, remove an existing product key, and force re-activation when an old key is stuck or a license needs to be rebound.
children.command:
cscript "C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\Office16\ospp.vbs" /dstatus
cscript "C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\Office16\ospp.vbs" /unpkey:XXXXX
steps: Open Command Prompt as Administrator
Navigate to the Office folder: cd "C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\Office16" (or Program Files (x86) for 32-bit Office on 64-bit Windows)
View current license: cscript ospp.vbs /dstatus — note the last 5 chars of the partial product key
Remove the key: cscript ospp.vbs /unpkey:XXXXX (replace XXXXX with those 5 chars)
Activate fresh: cscript ospp.vbs /inpkey:YOUR-NEW-KEY then cscript ospp.vbs /act
children.warning: Removing a key on a volume-licensed install can disable Office until you reactivate. Use only when troubleshooting a known activation issue.

children.name: Email Issues
children.description: Email problems across providers (Gmail, Outlook.com, iCloud) and clients (Apple Mail, Thunderbird), including server settings, authentication, deliverability, and bounces.

children.name: SMTP / IMAP / POP3 Basics
children.description: Standard email protocol port numbers — required to configure any email client manually.

children.name: SMTP Ports (25 / 465 / 587)
children.description: SMTP (outgoing mail) uses three ports depending on use case. Port 587 with STARTTLS is the modern recommended port for client-to-server email submission. Port 465 is legacy implicit SSL/TLS, still supported by most providers. Port 25 is for server-to-server relay and is widely blocked by ISPs.
children.command:
Port 587 — Submission (STARTTLS) — RECOMMENDED for clients
Port 465 — Legacy SMTPS (implicit TLS) — still works
Port 25  — Server-to-server relay — usually blocked by ISPs
Port 2525 — Alternative when others are blocked

children.name: IMAP Ports (143 / 993)
children.description: IMAP (incoming mail, keeps messages on the server) uses port 993 for SSL/TLS (recommended) or port 143 for plain/STARTTLS. Use 993 with SSL for any client setup today.
children.command:
Port 993 — IMAP over SSL/TLS — RECOMMENDED
Port 143 — IMAP plain (often upgraded via STARTTLS)

children.name: POP3 Ports (110 / 995)
children.description: POP3 (incoming mail, downloads then removes from server) uses port 995 for SSL/TLS (recommended) or port 110 for plain. Most email accounts should use IMAP instead — POP3 is only useful for single-device, offline-first setups.
children.command:
Port 995 — POP3 over SSL/TLS — RECOMMENDED
Port 110 — POP3 plain

children.name: Gmail
children.description: Google Gmail account, sync, and password issues.

children.name: Gmail App-Specific Passwords
children.description: App passwords are 16-character codes for connecting older apps (like classic Outlook or Thunderbird) to a Gmail account that has 2-Step Verification turned on. Google recommends 'Sign in with Google' instead when available, but app passwords still work.
steps: Turn on 2-Step Verification first: myaccount.google.com → Security → 2-Step Verification
Visit: myaccount.google.com/apppasswords
Enter a name like 'Outlook' → click Create
Copy the 16-character password shown (no spaces needed)
Paste it into your mail client's password field instead of your normal Google password
children.warning: Treat app passwords like full account passwords. Revoke any you don't recognize on the App passwords page.

children.name: Gmail IMAP / SMTP Server Settings
children.description: Standard server settings for connecting any email client to Gmail. Requires IMAP to be enabled in Gmail settings (it is by default) and an app password if 2-Step Verification is on.
children.command:
Incoming (IMAP)
  Server: imap.gmail.com
  Port: 993
  Security: SSL/TLS

Outgoing (SMTP)
  Server: smtp.gmail.com
  Port: 465 (SSL) or 587 (STARTTLS)
  Auth: Required
  Username: full Gmail address
  Password: app password (if 2SV on) or account password

children.name: Less Secure App Access (Removed)
children.description: Google removed the 'Less secure app access' option in 2022. Apps that used it (older Thunderbird, classic Outlook with basic auth) must now use either 'Sign in with Google' (OAuth) or an app-specific password. There is no way to re-enable LSA.
children.warning: If a client says 'authentication failed' since 2022 and there's no LSA setting visible anymore, switch to app passwords or update the client to a version that supports OAuth.

children.name: Recover Deleted Gmail (30-Day Window)
children.description: Deleted Gmail messages stay in Trash for 30 days. After 30 days they are permanently deleted and cannot be recovered. Drafts cannot be recovered from Trash at all.
steps: Open Gmail on the web
In the left sidebar, click More to expand → Trash (or Bin)
Check the box next to messages you want to recover
Click 'Move to' (folder icon) → choose Inbox or another label
Use search if you have many trashed messages: in:trash from:[sender]
children.warning: Past the 30-day window, only G Suite/Workspace admins (not personal Gmail users) can attempt server-side recovery — and only within 25 days of permanent deletion.

children.name: Outlook.com / Hotmail
children.description: Microsoft Outlook.com (webmail) account issues.

children.name: Outlook.com IMAP / SMTP Settings
children.description: Standard server settings for adding an Outlook.com / Hotmail / Live.com account to any third-party email client.
children.command:
Incoming (IMAP)
  Server: outlook.office365.com
  Port: 993
  Security: SSL/TLS

Outgoing (SMTP)
  Server: smtp-mail.outlook.com
  Port: 587
  Security: STARTTLS
  Auth: Required
  Username: full Outlook.com address
  Password: account password (or app password if 2SV)
children.warning: Microsoft has been migrating Outlook.com to require OAuth for third-party clients. Older clients using basic auth may fail and require an app password generated at account.live.com.

children.name: Outlook.com Sign-In Redirect Loop
children.description: After entering credentials, outlook.com redirects to the marketing page instead of the inbox. Caused by stale browser cache, cookies, or a Microsoft account state issue.
steps: Open the site in a private/incognito window → test login
Clear all cookies and site data for outlook.com and live.com
Sign in via account.microsoft.com first, then click 'Outlook' from the apps menu
Try a different browser to confirm the issue is browser-side
If persistent: sign in to account.live.com, check security alerts, complete any required identity verification

children.name: Apple Mail
children.description: Apple Mail (Mail.app) on macOS and iOS troubleshooting.

children.name: Stuck in Outbox / Won't Send
children.description: Mail message stays in Outbox with a clock or warning icon. Common causes: no internet, wrong SMTP server, or attachment over the size limit. Apple's recommended sequence: check connection, retry, then re-verify the outgoing server config.
steps: Open Mail → check the Outbox in the sidebar — if a message is there, the send failed
Verify you have internet (load a webpage in Safari)
Mail menu → Mailbox → 'Send' or 'Take All Accounts Online'
Mail menu → Settings → Accounts → select account → Server Settings → click 'Edit SMTP Server List' → verify Host Name, port (587), and authentication
On iPhone/iPad: Settings → Mail → Accounts → tap the account → tap SMTP under Outgoing Mail Server

children.name: Rebuild Mailbox (Apple Mail)
children.description: Rebuilding refreshes the local copy of a mailbox by erasing the cache and re-downloading from the server. Use when messages appear corrupted, are missing, or the mailbox shows the wrong message count.
steps: Open Mail
In the sidebar, click the mailbox/folder you want to rebuild
Menu bar → Mailbox → Rebuild
Wait for the process to finish — large mailboxes can take 30+ minutes
children.warning: Only works for IMAP/Exchange accounts where mail is on the server. POP3 accounts will lose any messages that were only stored locally.

children.name: Apple Mail Search Returns No Results
children.description: If Mail's search returns no results when you know the message exists, the Spotlight index for Mail is likely corrupted. Rebuild the Spotlight index for your home folder to fix it.
steps: System Settings → Spotlight (or Siri & Spotlight) → Search Privacy
Drag your home folder (or Macintosh HD) into the list — this removes it from indexing
Wait 10 seconds, then remove it from the list using the – button — this triggers re-indexing
Or via Terminal (faster): sudo mdutil -E /
Wait 1–2 hours for full re-index, then try Mail search again

children.name: Thunderbird
children.description: Mozilla Thunderbird email client troubleshooting.

children.name: Compact Folders (Reclaim Disk Space)
children.description: Thunderbird marks deleted messages but doesn't immediately remove them from disk. Compacting permanently removes them and shrinks the .msf files. Required periodically — large uncompacted folders can become corrupted.
steps: Right-click any folder in the folder list → 'Compact'
To compact all folders: File menu → 'Compact Folders' (or right-click the account name → 'Compact Folders')
Trust the 'Compact Folders' prompt when it appears — don't dismiss it repeatedly
children.warning: Do not interrupt compaction. Power loss or force-quit during compaction can corrupt folders. Back up the profile first if compacting a very large folder.

children.name: Reset Thunderbird Profile
children.description: Thunderbird profiles contain messages, account settings, address book, and add-ons. Creating a new profile resets the client to factory state. The old profile is preserved so you can recover data later.
steps: Quit Thunderbird completely
Open the Profile Manager: Win+R → type: thunderbird.exe -P → Enter (Mac: /Applications/Thunderbird.app/Contents/MacOS/thunderbird -P from Terminal)
Uncheck 'Use the selected profile without asking at startup'
Click 'Create Profile...' → follow the wizard → choose 'default-new' or similar name
Launch with the new profile — reconfigure accounts from scratch
Old profile remains in %appdata%\Thunderbird\Profiles\ (Windows) or ~/Library/Thunderbird/Profiles/ (Mac) for recovery

children.name: iCloud Mail
children.description: Apple iCloud Mail account issues.

children.name: iCloud App-Specific Password
children.description: To use iCloud Mail in any non-Apple email client (Thunderbird, Outlook, etc.), generate an app-specific password from account.apple.com. Required even on Apple devices when third-party apps need iCloud access.
steps: Sign in at account.apple.com
In the Sign-In and Security section, select 'App-Specific Passwords'
Click '+' or 'Generate an app-specific password'
Enter a label like 'Thunderbird' → Create
Copy the password and paste it as the password in your email client (paired with your full @icloud.com address as username)
children.warning: Requires two-factor authentication on your Apple Account. App-specific passwords can be revoked individually from the same page.

children.name: iCloud Mail Stops Receiving on iPhone
children.description: iPhone shows old mail but doesn't receive new messages. Common causes: Mail Days to Sync set too low, the iCloud Mail toggle is off, or the iCloud account hit its storage limit (sender will see 'mailbox full' bounce).
steps: Check iCloud storage: Settings → [your name] → iCloud → Manage Account Storage — if full, free space or upgrade
Verify Mail is enabled for iCloud: Settings → [your name] → iCloud → See All → Mail → toggle on
Sign out and back in to iCloud Mail: Settings → Mail → Accounts → iCloud → tap account → Delete → re-add
Restart iPhone
Try iCloud Mail at icloud.com in a browser to verify the messages are at least arriving at the server

children.name: Deliverability & Bounces
children.description: Why emails bounce, go to spam, or fail authentication checks.

children.name: 550 Mailbox Unavailable
children.description: A 550 SMTP bounce with 'mailbox unavailable' means the recipient's mail server rejected the message. Most common cause: the address doesn't exist (typo) or was disabled. Other causes: recipient over quota, sender blacklisted, content filtering.
steps: Verify the recipient address character-by-character — a typo is the most common cause
Check if you're sending from a blacklisted IP (use mxtoolbox.com or similar)
If the bounce mentions 'quota' or 'over quota', the recipient mailbox is full — they need to delete messages
If sending in bulk: check SPF/DKIM/DMARC alignment (see related node)
If sending from a personal account: try from a different account to isolate the issue

children.name: SPF / DKIM / DMARC Quick Check
children.description: Modern email providers (Gmail, Outlook) require sending domains to publish SPF, DKIM, and DMARC DNS records or messages risk being marked spam or rejected. Use a free checker to verify your domain's records.
steps: Visit a free DMARC checker like easydmarc.com/tools/dmarc-lookup or mxtoolbox.com/dmarc.aspx
Enter your sending domain (e.g. example.com)
Verify the SPF record exists and includes all your sending services (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, mailgun, etc.)
Verify a DKIM selector record exists for each sender (e.g. google._domainkey.example.com)
Verify _dmarc.example.com publishes a DMARC policy (p=none for monitoring, p=quarantine or p=reject for enforcement)

children.name: Email Going to Spam
children.description: Your legitimate email gets filtered to recipients' spam folders. Causes are almost always sender-side: missing authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC), low sender reputation, spammy content, or sending from a shared IP with a bad neighbor.
steps: Verify SPF, DKIM, and DMARC are configured for your sending domain (see related node)
Avoid spam-trigger words in subject lines (FREE!, WINNER, $$$, all-caps)
Check your sender reputation at senderscore.org or talosintelligence.com
If sending from your own server: warm up the IP slowly over weeks — don't blast 10,000 emails on day one
Ask recipients to add your address to their contacts (whitelists your sender)
If using a marketing platform: check your bounce rate and unsubscribe rate are below industry averages
